purpose: Primary-source evidence register for Asian aviation-fuel resilience research. All evidence is separated from model assumptions and inferred policy implications.

sources.title: Southeast Asia Energy Outlook 2026 — Executive summary
sources.measurementPeriod: Pre-crisis exposure described in the 2026 report; exact exposure measurement year not specified in executive summary.
claims: Before the 2026 crisis, roughly 60% of Southeast Asian crude imports came from the Middle East; 45% of oil-product supply depended on Middle Eastern crude.
Many regional refineries process medium/heavy Gulf crudes, limiting rapid feedstock substitution.
The report recommends coordinated stockholding and emergency responses.
limitations: Regional oil-system evidence, not airport Jet A-1 inventory, contract-price or airline-specific data.
Scenarios reflect pre-crisis policy settings and are exploratory, not forecasts.
Do not label these regional exposure percentages as each airport's vulnerability.
sources.analyticalImplication: Changing airport or regional fuel seller may leave an airline exposed to the same upstream supply shock.
sources.verified: Full official HTML, executive-summary lines 65–81; publication date from report landing page.

sources.title: World Oil Transit Chokepoints
claims: Hormuz carried 20.9 million barrels/day of oil in 1H2025; 89% of its crude-and-condensate flows went to Asian markets.
China, India, Japan and South Korea together received 74% of Hormuz crude-and-condensate flows in 1H2025.
Malacca carried 23.2 million barrels/day of oil in 1H2025, 29% of global maritime oil flows.
Malacca links Middle Eastern suppliers to East/Southeast Asia; Gulf OPEC producers provided nearly 60% of its crude flows.
limitations: Historical tanker-tracking estimates; not current traffic, jet-fuel flows or probabilities of disruption.
Asia includes South Asia; 89% applies to crude plus condensate, not all petroleum.
Flow estimates were revised: use this March 2026 edition consistently rather than mixing it with June 2025 figures.
sources.analyticalImplication: Analyse Gulf chokepoints through Asian importer exposure; scenarios at connected airports should allow correlated shocks.
sources.verified: Full official HTML, updated date and tables; EIA calculations using Vortexa and February 2026 STEO.

sources.title: Think Paper #1 — Fuel Tankering: economic benefits and environmental impact
sources.measurementPeriod: June 2018 ECAC traffic sample, annualised; February 2019 fuel-price reference.
claims: BADA simulations estimated annual ECAC tankering could burn 286,000 additional tonnes of fuel, emit 901,000 tonnes of CO2, and generate EUR265 million net airline savings.
The simulation incorporated aircraft performance, maximum takeoff/landing weights, tank capacity and legal fuel minima.
Price variation reflects negotiated contracts, geography, distribution, quantities and supplier competition.
limitations: European model estimates, not observed Asia-wide behaviour or a current savings forecast.
Only two airlines' negotiated prices at 140 airports; aircraft models covered 66% of ECAC traffic before extrapolation.
Excluded multi-leg tankering and non-price motivations; do not transfer its parameter calibration mechanically to an Asian route.
sources.analyticalImplication: Cost-minimising tankering can increase physical fuel consumption; model mass-dependent burn and report emissions beside savings.
sources.verified: Full official eight-page PDF and dated publication landing page; pp.1–5.

sources.publisher: AFSC Operations Limited / AFSC Refuelling Limited
sources.title: The Facility
sources.publicationDateNote: Undated operator page; copyright range is not a publication date.
sources.measurementPeriod: Facility specification on page accessed 12 November 2026; specification effective date not given.
claims: The on-airport system lists 12 tanks with aggregate capacity 220,000 cubic metres.
Sha Chau's twin berth can accommodate barges up to 6,000 dwt and serves as emergency backup to the Permanent Aviation Fuel Facility.
The airport system includes apron hydrants; Airport Authority franchises operations to AFSC.
limitations: Installed capacity is not current stock, usable inventory or days of cover.
Do not infer a single point of failure: the source explicitly identifies an emergency backup.
No current throughput, replenishment time, vendor-specific inventory or prices are disclosed.
sources.analyticalImplication: Airport resilience depends on certified storage, receipt routes and hydrant delivery, not solely national aggregate oil reserves.
sources.verified: Full operator HTML, facility section, lines 15–29.

sources.title: CAAS Sets Out Criteria for Sustainable Aviation Fuel to be Procured and Uplifted on Flights from Singapore
sources.measurementPeriod: Policy announcement: initial tender planned by mid-December 2026; deliveries from June 2027.
claims: SAFCo's first levy-funded tender is planned for 20–30 kilotonnes, using a portfolio of term contracts and spot purchases.
Bid assessment includes price, supply-chain resilience, delivery certainty and sustainability documentation.
Qualifying fuel must meet CORSIA eligibility and at least 40% lifecycle emissions reduction; deliveries must use Changi's existing fuel hydrant infrastructure.
limitations: Future tender and deliveries, not fuel already procured or uplifted by the research cutoff.
SAF lifecycle reduction is not zero tailpipe emissions.
This is SAF procurement governance, not public conventional Jet A-1 airport pricing.
sources.analyticalImplication: A credible security recommendation already has a regional precedent: assess delivery resilience alongside price, with traceable certification.
sources.dateClarification: The footer update date is not established as the article revision date; article publication is 5 November 2026.

sources.title: Oil security and emergency response
sources.publicationDateNote: Undated living institutional page; includes March 2026 collective action.
sources.measurementPeriod: Institutional stockholding rules as accessed 12 November 2026.
claims: IEA countries with a stockholding obligation must maintain stocks equivalent to at least 90 days of net oil imports.
Stocks may include crude or refined products, public and commercial holdings, and some stocks held abroad under bilateral guarantees.
IEA recommends sufficient refined-product stocks and timely emergency drawdown/distribution; its minimum does not prescribe crude versus refined shares.
limitations: Net exporters have no IEP stockholding obligation.
The 90-day denominator is net oil imports, not total consumption or airport jet demand.
A national aggregate stockholding figure cannot establish aviation fuel availability at a particular airport.
sources.analyticalImplication: National reserve compliance and local operational fuel resilience require separate indicators and must never be represented by a single interchangeable 'days cover' figure.
sources.verified: Full official HTML, stockholding FAQ and policy sections.

sources.title: IEA confirms Member country contributions to collective action to release oil stocks in response to Middle East disruptions
sources.measurementPeriod: Commitments to collective action agreed 11 March 2026, reported as of 19 March 2026.
claims: Members agreed on 11 March to make 400 million barrels available; initial volumes had begun to reach the market by the 19 March announcement.
The provisional country table totals 426 million barrels including production increases; Japan's contribution is 79.8 million barrels and Korea's 22.5 million.
Most contributions are crude; European contributions are mainly refined products.
limitations: Commitments and initial availability are not cumulative delivered volumes.
Provisional composition is explicitly subject to change.
Refined products are not synonymous with jet fuel; source cannot establish current November 2026 shipping status.
sources.analyticalImplication: The 2026 research context includes an actual supply disruption and coordinated intervention. Model scenarios must be labelled counterfactual severity tests, not falsely presented as the first hypothetical instance of disruption.
sources.verified: Full official media release, date and country table.

sources.title: RefuelEU aviation initiative: Council adopts new law to decarbonise the aviation sector
sources.measurementPeriod: Regulatory design adopted 2023; core uplift obligation applies from 1 January 2025.
claims: The operator's yearly fuel uplift at a given Union airport must be at least 90% of yearly fuel required, targeting emissions from tankering extra weight.
The legislation combines this demand-side rule with SAF supply requirements and reporting.
limitations: Annual operator-by-airport measure, not 90% on each flight.
Applies within defined EU scope; it is not an Asian legal requirement.
For detailed safety and supply exemptions consult Regulation (EU) 2023/2405 Article 5 and Commission guidance; the press release is an official summary, not the operative legal text.
sources.analyticalImplication: Policy should distinguish economic tankering from justified contingency fuel and identify the scale at which incentives and exemptions operate.
sources.verified: Full Council press release; current scope corroborated by official Commission FAQ.

sources.title: CORSIA frequently asked questions — 3.59–3.62
sources.publicationDateNote: Undated living FAQ; date of individual conversion-factor passage not provided.
sources.measurementPeriod: Accounting method, not an empirical observation period.
claims: Jet A and Jet A-1 fuel mass is converted to combustion CO2 using 3.16 kg CO2 per kg fuel.
CORSIA permits actual density or standard 0.8 kg/litre when converting fuel volume to mass, with method documented.
limitations: Combustion CO2 excludes fuel-production lifecycle emissions and aviation non-CO2 warming effects.
Standard density is an accounting convention, not a measurement of a particular fuel batch.
A carbon-price sensitivity is a model assumption unless linked to the operator's applicable real compliance cost.
sources.analyticalImplication: Expose unit conversions and label emissions as combustion CO2; do not mix tonnes, litres, US gallons and CO2-equivalent.

sources.title: Petroleum spot-price definitions, sources and explanatory notes
sources.measurementPeriod: Market-series definition, not a current price observation.
claims: A spot price concerns one immediate-delivery transaction at a specified quantity and location.
EIA's U.S. Gulf Coast geography refers to ports on the Texas/Louisiana coast.
Kerosene-type jet fuel is a defined aviation petroleum product; a crude marker is a different commodity.
limitations: A U.S. Gulf Coast benchmark is not a Singapore, Hong Kong or Tokyo into-plane quotation.
No airport premium, handling, tax, credit, contract discount or fuel availability is disclosed by this series definition.
Refresh time must be distinct from observation date; latest available daily data are delayed, not tick-by-tick executable prices.
sources.analyticalImplication: Public prices may anchor a market-monitoring panel. Airline decisions require comparable, timestamped airport-specific contract quotes; otherwise show scenario prices and no trade recommendation.
sources.verified: Full official definitions HTML, spot-price and geography entries.

sources.title: ReFuelEU Aviation Annual Technical Report 2026 — 2025 in review
sources.measurementPeriod: 2025 reported EU fuel supply and SAF; 2026 publication with corrigendum.
claims: Reported 2025 supply includes 1.1 million tonnes SAF within 39.3 million tonnes aviation fuel; 90% of suppliers reported.
EASA reports 85% of SAF feedstocks imported, with China, Malaysia and Indonesia prominent.
Published annual reference prices are EUR1,925/tonne SAF versus EUR640/tonne conventional jet fuel.
limitations: EU reporting sample and annual reference prices, not Asian airport quotes.
November 2026 corrigendum clarifies production and import-statistics interpretation; use the updated report.
Feedstock origin is distinct from fuel production location and procurement seller; do not treat these as interchangeable concentration measures.
sources.analyticalImplication: SAF can change the geography of import dependence rather than eliminate it. Security assessment should trace feedstock, production, certification and delivery constraints separately.
sources.verified: Full official publication landing page, dated summary and corrigendum; full report not needed for these explicitly listed facts.

keyFindings: Tankering reallocates the place/time of an airline's purchases; it does not create fuel. Extra carried mass increases total consumption.
Private cost reduction, airline continuity, airport system resilience and national energy security are different outcomes and need separate metrics.
Upstream Gulf crude exposure can correlate shortages across otherwise diverse Asian refuelling locations.
Crude-stock barrels, installed airport capacity and certified usable Jet A-1 inventory are not interchangeable.
Public benchmark freshness does not establish airport price comparability or executability.
SAF procurement and emissions policy interact with security; resilience criteria, lifecycle accounting and imported feedstock dependence all matter.
Use 2026 primary-source updates and clearly date historical exposures. Current disruption status cannot be inferred from a March announcement.
